problem: Classical planners treat humans as moving obstacles and simulation-trained learned policies rarely transfer the social subtlety (yielding, slowing) needed for comfortable co-existence with people in real buildings.
motivation: Mobile robots in hospitals, warehouses and shared workspaces must navigate with people, not just around them. Pre-trained VLA models give general navigation, but specializing them on few in-situ demonstrations risks degrading general navigation ability.
key_idea: Keep a frozen VLA navigation backbone and add a lightweight multiplicative-gating yield head, trained from fewer than 20 demonstrations with balanced embedding replay and a proxemic safety regularizer, so it can only attenuate velocity.
insight: The multiplicative gating guarantees the head can only slow the base policy, never accelerate or redirect it, which gives structural safety. The ablation shows balanced replay is essential: removing it causes an 18.4% drop in navigation success because the robot becomes overly cautious. Trajectory prediction and gaze features each also contribute (per the abstract's ablations).
method: Frozen VLA backbone: predicts coarse velocity commands from ego-centric RGB and a natural-language navigation goal
Yield policy head: lightweight module that modulates the commands using human proximity, gaze direction and predicted pedestrian trajectory
Multiplicative gating: the output scales the base velocity so it can only attenuate, never accelerate or redirect
Balanced replay buffer: stores compact backbone embeddings from navigation and yielding episodes and samples them in balanced proportions to prevent forgetting
Social safety regularizer: penalizes trajectories that enter the intimate proxemic zone
Deakin-Social-Nav dataset: 6 h of annotated ego-centric data with 412 human encounters and 187 comfort surveys

setting.training_data: Fewer than 20 in-situ demonstrations collected during normal building operation, plus replayed navigation-episode embeddings
setting.observation: Ego-centric monocular RGB + language goal, with detected human proximity, gaze and predicted pedestrian trajectory

numbers_note: Abstract only; results given are non-benchmark (real-world, Deakin-Social-Nav): 96.7% navigation success, 61% fewer close passes (<0.5 m), comfort 4.4/5 with 28 participants, replay removal causes an 18.4% success drop. No canonical benchmark table.
results: On a Clearpath TurtleBot 4 in two Deakin University buildings with natural pedestrian traffic, the method reduces close passes (<0.5 m) by 61% versus baselines with comparable goal-reach times and a 96.7% success rate. Participants (n=28) rated comfort 4.4/5, significantly above classical and learning-based social navigation baselines.
limitations: Evaluated only on one robot platform at two buildings of a single campus, with a small demonstration set
Only abstract available; the identity of the VLA backbone and the baselines is unspecified, and the yield head only attenuates so it cannot actively avoid people
builds_on: Memory-efficient VLA specialization with embedding replay
